analysis.one_liner: Locks in rising federal funding until Washington pays its promised 40% share of special education costs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 138 cosponsors to raise federal special education funding to the promised 40% share of costs died in the House Education and Labor Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make federal special education funding permanent and automatic, ramping up from roughly a 15% share of costs to the 40% share Congress promised in 1975 — about $49 billion a year by 2031. It had 138 cosponsors, including 11 Republicans, but was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the term ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Students with disabilities and their families, public school districts, and state and local taxpayers. Today the federal government pays only a fraction of the special education costs it promised to cover in 1975, so school districts make up the gap with local property taxes, program cuts, and staff shortages. The bill would replace the yearly appropriations fight with a mandatory funding formula tied to the number of children served and average per-pupil costs, reaching full funding in 2031.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students with disabilities and public school districts

how_it_helps.text: Converts federal special education grants from yearly, discretionary appropriations into permanent, mandatory funding that cannot lapse if Congress fails to pass a spending bill.

Ramps up the federal share over ten years — from about $2.6 billion in fiscal 2022 to $49.4 billion in fiscal 2031 — until the federal government covers 40% of the average per-pupil cost for each child served, the level promised when the law passed in 1975.

Ties the funding formula directly to the number of children receiving special education services and national average per-pupil spending, so money grows automatically with enrollment and costs rather than depending on annual political decisions.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill identifies no revenue source for the new spending; it states the appropriations must be consistent with pay-as-you-go budget rules, meaning the tens of billions in new mandatory spending would have to be offset by spending cuts or tax increases elsewhere, or it would trigger automatic across-the-board reductions under those rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; no revenue source specified

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no funding source. By fiscal 2031 it commits roughly $49 billion a year in new mandatory spending, and Section 3 requires it to comply with pay-as-you-go rules — so Congress would need to cut other programs or raise revenue to pay for it, or the rules would force automatic spending reductions across the budget.

Making the funding permanent and mandatory removes Congress's ability to adjust it during budget crises, a real constraint that fiscal hawks in both parties have used to argue against full IDEA funding for decades.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: tens of billions of dollars a year reaching the classrooms where districts currently pay the federal government's unpaid share. The cost is equally real — a permanent $49 billion annual commitment with no specified offsets, which either adds to deficits or forces cuts and tax changes elsewhere. The bill's honest weakness is that it never answers the who-pays question; its honest strength is that it finally enforces a 47-year-old promise.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and died there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on November 16, 2021, with 17 original cosponsors from both parties.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which took no further action on it.

Over the following 13 months the bill gained 138 cosponsors — 127 Democrats and 11 Republicans — but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo. School districts and local taxpayers keep covering the roughly 40-point federal shortfall in special education funding, and the Appropriations Committee keeps deciding the federal special education share year by year instead of it being automatic.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; districts keep covering the federal shortfall

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Democratic — 127 of 138 cosponsors — but 11 Republicans signed on and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows a bill stalled in committee rather than a party-line floor fight.

industries.note: The bill would raise the federal share of special education costs toward 40% of per-pupil spending, freeing local dollars that districts now divert from general programs and property taxes to cover the federal shortfall. Districts currently receive roughly $2.6 billion of the incremental ramp in fiscal 2022 alone.
Because districts make up the unfunded federal share from local and state sources, full federal funding would shift billions of dollars a year off state and local budgets.
